title: Resource Management: Food, Water & Energy in the UK
description: Why food miles, water transfer and a changing energy mix are reshaping UK supply.
content_html:
Why Resources Matter

Food, water and energy are the three resources every country needs to keep working. Without enough of any one of them, businesses close, hospitals struggle and people go hungry. Geographers call the way societies plan, share and protect these essentials resource management. The UK has plentiful supplies of fresh water and a developed economy that can buy what it does not grow, but its supply systems are changing fast as imports rise, water demand shifts and the energy mix moves away from fossil fuels.

Key Fact

The UK now imports nearly half its food, transfers water from the wet north and west to the dry south-east, and has shifted its electricity generation from over 70% coal in 1990 to over 40% renewables today.

Food in the UK

In 1984 the UK produced around 78% of the food it consumed. Today that figure is closer to 60% — meaning over 40% is imported. Demand has changed: shoppers expect strawberries in December and avocados year-round. Add modern lifestyles that prefer ready meals, and the result is rising food miles — the distance food travels from farm to plate.

Year-round demand for ‘summer’ produce means UK supermarkets fly green beans from Kenya, mangetout from Peru and tomatoes from Spain. Each step adds to the carbon footprint, so movements such as ‘Buy British’, farmers’ markets and farm shops have grown in response. Many supermarkets now label produce with country-of-origin and carbon scores, and some chefs have built menus around seasonal British vegetables to push back against airfreighted imports.

Two further trends shape UK food supply:

  • Agribusiness: the rise of large-scale, highly mechanised farms producing cereals and dairy efficiently — but with concerns over biodiversity loss, fertiliser run-off and animal welfare.
  • Local sourcing: a movement toward shorter supply chains that supports rural economies and lowers food miles, though prices are usually higher.

Water in the UK

The UK has plenty of water overall — but it is not in the right places. Over half of UK rainfall falls on the north and west, while two-thirds of the population lives in the drier south and east. Areas of water deficit include London, the East Midlands and East Anglia, where less than 700 mm of rain falls a year. Areas of water surplus include western Scotland, the Lake District and Wales, with over 2,000 mm a year.

To match supply to demand, the UK relies on water transfer schemes. The Kielder Water reservoir in Northumberland (the largest in the UK) sends water south through the Tyne, while the Elan Valley in mid-Wales has supplied Birmingham since 1904. Demand keeps rising as population grows and people use more water at home (washing machines, dishwashers, gardens). Quality is also a challenge — agricultural run-off, sewage discharges and microplastics put pressure on water companies to clean water before it reaches taps and rivers.

Energy in the UK

The UK’s energy mix has changed dramatically. In 1990 coal generated over 70% of UK electricity; in 2024 less than 1%. The last coal-fired power station, Ratcliffe-on-Soar, closed in late 2024. Today the mix is roughly:

  • Renewables (over 40%): wind (especially North Sea offshore farms like Hornsea), solar, hydro and biomass.
  • Natural gas (around 30–35%): still the largest single source, used in ‘peaking’ power stations that fill gaps when wind drops.
  • Nuclear (around 12–15%): from stations such as Sizewell B and Hinkley Point B (the last reactor closed in 2022); Hinkley Point C is under construction.
  • Imports and other: via interconnectors with France, Norway and the Netherlands.
Key Fact

UK domestic supplies of coal, gas and oil are all in decline. North Sea oil and gas peaked around 1999 and now produces less than half its peak volume, leaving the UK increasingly reliant on imports and renewable generation.

Economic and Environmental Trade-offs

Every energy choice has both economic and environmental costs. Fossil-fuel extraction creates jobs and tax revenue but warms the climate; nuclear is low-carbon but produces radioactive waste and is expensive to build; wind farms are clean but face local opposition over views, bird strikes and turbine noise. Some areas with surviving North Sea oil and gas (Aberdeen) depend heavily on the industry for skilled jobs, while areas with new offshore wind (Hull, Grimsby) are emerging as a green industrial cluster. Resource policy is rarely just about engineering — it is also about employment, regional balance and climate commitments.

In 2019 the UK was the first major economy to commit by law to reach net-zero greenhouse-gas emissions by 2050. That target shapes resource policy across food (lower-carbon farming), water (energy used for treatment) and energy (rapid expansion of wind and solar). Interim targets include reaching net-zero electricity by around 2035. The pace of change here is faster than almost any other country — though the cost and the impact on workers in fossil-fuel industries remain contested.

Why This Matters

A high-income country can be food, water and energy insecure too. The UK’s rising food imports, growing water transfers and shifting energy mix all show how the modern resource challenge is no longer just about scarcity — it is about sustainability, climate change and security of supply. The next two lessons zoom out to the global picture and then close with one community renewable scheme that shows what sustainable energy can look like at small scale.
exam_tip_html: For 4-mark ‘Explain’ questions on the UK’s changing energy mix, link a specific shift to a clear cause: ‘Coal generation fell from over 70% in 1990 to under 1% in 2024 because of climate policy and falling renewable costs.’ For 6-mark ‘Suggest’ questions on water transfer schemes, name a real example (Kielder Water, Elan Valley) and explain both an advantage (matches surplus to deficit) and a disadvantage (high cost, environmental impact). Examiners reward specific places, dates and figures over vague claims.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • UK food self-sufficiency has fallen from around 78% in 1984 to about 60% today, raising food miles and pushing back movements like local sourcing and seasonal eating.
  • UK water demand is concentrated in the dry south-east while supply is in the wet north and west, so transfers from Kielder Water and Elan Valley are essential.
  • The UK’s energy mix has shifted from over 70% coal in 1990 to over 40% renewables today, though imports and natural gas remain important and nuclear capacity is being rebuilt at Hinkley Point C.

glossary_terms.definition: The way societies and governments plan, supply and protect food, water and energy resources to meet demand sustainably.
The distance food travels from where it is produced to where it is eaten, often used as an indicator of the carbon footprint of food.
The movement of water from areas of surplus to areas of deficit, often through pipelines, canals or rivers.
The combination of different sources of energy — fossil fuels, renewables and nuclear — that a country uses to meet its electricity and heating needs.

practice_questions.text: Assess the view that imports are now the biggest threat to UK resource security.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: balanced argument acknowledging the scale of imports (food self-sufficiency falling, gas and oil increasingly imported, electricity interconnectors with France and Norway) but evaluating other threats (climate change altering rainfall patterns, ageing nuclear stations, rising domestic demand, biodiversity loss in farmland). Reaches a justified judgement (e.g. ‘imports raise vulnerability, but climate change is a deeper structural threat’). Secure: two-sided argument with one or two factors weighed. Developing: lists threats with limited evaluation. Emerging: agrees or disagrees without weighing alternatives.

title: Global Energy: Surplus, Deficit & Insecurity
description: Why energy demand is rising, what affects supply, and the consequences of energy insecurity.
content_html:
Energy: Why Demand Keeps Rising

Global energy use has roughly doubled since 1980 and shows no sign of stopping. Three main drivers explain why. Economic development raises living standards: as countries industrialise, factories, transport and air conditioning consume more power. Rising population simply means more people to feed, light and move — the world reached 8 billion in 2022 and is forecast to reach over 9.5 billion by 2050. Technology creates new demand: data centres for streaming and AI, electric vehicles and bigger fridges all consume more electricity than the equipment they replace.

Key Fact

Three drivers of rising global energy demand: economic development (industrialisation in China and India), population growth (world reached 8 billion in 2022), and technology (data centres, electric vehicles and air conditioning). Together they push demand upward by roughly 1–2% a year.

Where Energy Is — and Where It Is Used

Energy supply does not match demand. The wealthy regions of North America, Europe, the Gulf and East Asia consume the most energy per person, while sub-Saharan Africa and parts of South Asia use the least. Yet many of the largest reserves sit in countries that consume relatively little: roughly 50% of the world’s known oil reserves lie in the Middle East, while Russia, Qatar and the United States hold the largest natural gas reserves. This mismatch creates global trade in energy — oil tankers crossing the Indian Ocean, gas pipelines crossing Eurasia, electricity flowing across European interconnectors.

A typical American consumes around 75 megawatt-hours of energy a year — roughly ten times the figure for a typical Indian and a hundred times that of someone living in rural Ethiopia. As poorer regions develop, their per-person demand will rise sharply, even if total population growth slows. Climate-policy debates often centre on whether richer countries should reduce their high consumption while emerging economies catch up.

Surplus, Deficit and Energy Security

Geographers describe countries as having an energy surplus when they produce more than they use, or an energy deficit when they produce less. Saudi Arabia, Russia, Norway and Qatar are surplus countries that export oil and gas. Japan, the UK and Germany are deficit countries that depend on imports. Energy security is the goal: enough energy, reliably available, at a price an economy can afford.

Factors Affecting Energy Supply

Energy supply is shaped by several factors:

  • Physical: climate (sun for solar, wind speeds), geology (oil and gas formations, suitable rivers for hydro), and the existence of reserves (Saudi oil, Norwegian gas, Icelandic geothermal).
  • Cost of exploitation: oil from shallow Gulf wells is cheap to extract; deep-water Atlantic oil and Canadian tar sands cost two to three times as much per barrel.
  • Technology: hydraulic fracturing (‘fracking’) unlocked US shale gas; modern wind turbines have made offshore wind cheaper than gas in the UK.
  • Political factors: wars and sanctions (the 2022 invasion of Ukraine cut Russian gas to Europe), nationalisation of resources (Venezuela), or political alliances (the OPEC group of oil-exporting countries) can rapidly change supply.

Consequences of Energy Insecurity

When supply does not meet demand, the consequences ripple through whole economies and ecosystems. Five impacts are commonly listed:

  • Exploration of difficult areas: insecurity drives drilling into the Arctic, the deep Atlantic and tar sands — risky, expensive and damaging to fragile ecosystems.
  • Economic costs: when fuel is short, prices spike. UK gas prices in 2022 reached over five times their 2020 level, raising costs for households and factories alike.
  • Environmental costs: turning to alternatives like coal, lignite or burning wood imports raises air pollution and greenhouse-gas emissions.
  • Food production: modern farming depends on fertilisers, irrigation pumps and refrigeration. Energy shocks raise food prices — the 2022 spike pushed up bread, milk and meat costs across Europe.
  • Industrial output: factories close or cut hours when energy is rationed. UK steelworks, ceramics and chemical plants warned of closures during the 2022–23 gas crisis.

In some cases, severe insecurity drives conflict between countries over disputed pipelines, oil fields or electricity infrastructure.

Before 2022, Europe imported around 40% of its natural gas from Russia. After Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the EU committed to cutting Russian gas drastically, while sanctions and pipeline sabotage (Nord Stream) cut flow further. Wholesale gas prices in Europe rose more than fivefold in 2022, fuel poverty surged, and governments rushed to find alternative supplies (US LNG, Norwegian pipelines, Qatari gas) and to accelerate renewable-energy roll-out. The crisis showed how quickly energy security can be rewritten by political events.

Key Fact

Energy insecurity drives rising prices for households, slowing factories, falling food output, exploration in fragile regions like the Arctic and, in extreme cases, conflict between rival states.

Why This Matters

Global energy use sits at the heart of three of the biggest stories of the 21st century: climate change, geopolitical conflict, and the rise of electric and digital economies. Understanding why demand is rising, where supply sits and what insecurity does to people prepares you for the final lesson, which moves from the global picture to a single small-scale renewable scheme that shows what a low-carbon energy future can look like.
exam_tip_html: For 6-mark ‘Suggest’ questions on impacts of energy insecurity, give specific examples (UK gas prices in 2022, drilling in the Arctic) rather than general claims. For 9-mark ‘Assess’ questions on factors affecting supply, weigh up at least two factors (physical vs political, or cost vs technology) and reach a clear judgement — markers reward a clear answer to the question, not just a balanced description.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Global energy demand is rising because of economic development, population growth and new technology — with the world reaching 8 billion people in 2022.
  • Supply is shaped by physical, cost, technology and political factors — the 2022 Russian gas crisis showed how quickly politics can disrupt supply.
  • Energy insecurity raises prices, harms food and industry, drives risky exploration and can fuel conflict — making the move toward sustainable supply urgent.

glossary_terms.definition: A country whose own production of energy exceeds the amount it consumes, allowing it to export the surplus.
A country whose own production of energy falls short of what it consumes, leaving it dependent on imports.
The reliable, affordable access to enough energy to meet a country's needs without sudden disruption.

title: Sustainable Energy: Renewables & a Local LIC Scheme
description: Renewable and non-renewable sources and how a community micro-hydro scheme cuts poverty.
content_html:
Two Families of Energy

Almost every form of energy used today fits into one of two families. Renewable energy comes from sources that replenish naturally and quickly — sunlight, wind, flowing water, tides, geothermal heat and biomass. Non-renewable energy comes from sources that take millions of years to form and cannot be replaced on a human timescale — coal, oil, natural gas and the uranium used in nuclear plants. The world’s energy mix is gradually shifting from non-renewable to renewable sources, but the change is uneven and contested.

Key Fact

Seven main renewables — biomass, wind, hydro, tidal, geothermal, wave and solar — replenish naturally. Non-renewables include coal, oil and natural gas (fossil fuels) and uranium for nuclear power. Around 30% of world electricity now comes from renewables, up from under 20% in 2010.

Renewable Energy Sources

Each renewable source has its own strengths and weaknesses:

  • Wind: grows fastest where wind speeds are reliable. Turbines work well off coastlines (the UK’s North Sea farms) but face local opposition over views and noise.
  • Solar: photovoltaic panels generate electricity from sunlight. Costs fell over 80% in the last decade, making solar the cheapest new electricity in many countries. India and China lead in installed capacity.
  • Hydro: dams trap river water and release it through turbines. Reliable but disrupts ecosystems and can displace communities (e.g. China’s Three Gorges Dam).
  • Tidal and wave: exploit the rise and fall of the sea or breaking waves. Predictable but expensive to engineer.
  • Geothermal: taps underground heat. Iceland gets around 65% of its primary energy this way; the UK has very limited capacity.
  • Biomass: burning wood, crops or organic waste. Counted as renewable if regrown, but can compete with food production and produces local air pollution.

Non-Renewable Energy Sources

Fossil fuels still supply over half of global energy. Coal remains the leading source of electricity in China and India because it is cheap and abundant, despite the highest carbon emissions per unit. Oil dominates transport — petrol, diesel and aviation fuel — though electric vehicles are growing fast. Natural gas is the cleanest fossil fuel, used widely for heating and electricity. Nuclear from uranium produces low-carbon electricity but raises concerns over waste storage, accidents (Chernobyl 1986, Fukushima 2011) and the high cost of building new plants.

Oil, gas and coal stay popular for several reasons. They have very high energy density (a litre of diesel carries enormous power for its size), the infrastructure for extracting, refining and burning them is already built, and they are reliable on demand — unlike wind or solar, you can turn them on whenever you need power. Replacing them takes both time and trillions of dollars in new grids, batteries and electric transport. Even with rapid renewable growth, fossil fuels are likely to play a role for decades.

A Local Renewable Scheme: Chambamontera, Peru

For the AQA case study of a local renewable scheme in an LIC or NEE, this lesson uses the Chambamontera micro-hydro scheme in northern Peru, completed in 2010. Around 60 mountainous farming villages in this region had no grid electricity. Micro-hydro uses a stream’s natural fall to spin a small turbine. The scheme provides:

  • Power for around 60 households in a community with annual income of just £700–1,400 per family.
  • A 20-year lifespan with low running costs, making it affordable in the long term.
  • Local ownership and maintenance — villagers were trained by the NGO Practical Action to run and repair the system, building local skills.
  • Environmental sustainability — uses river flow, not stored water, so there is no large reservoir flooding farmland or displacing people.
Key Fact

Chambamontera (Peru) cost around £43,000 funded mainly by Practical Action and the Peruvian government. It pays for itself by lifting incomes — villagers can refrigerate produce, charge tools and study after dark, raising productivity and quality of life.

Why Chambamontera Reduces Poverty

Electricity is more than a convenience — it is a poverty trap broken. Before the scheme, families used candles and kerosene (expensive, polluting and a fire risk). Children could not study after dark. Coffee farmers had to sell beans wet and at low prices because they could not refrigerate or grind them locally. After the scheme:

  • Education improved as schools and homes had reliable lighting for evening study.
  • Health improved as kerosene fumes (a major cause of respiratory illness) disappeared from homes.
  • Income rose — farmers could process coffee on-site and sell at higher prices, reducing reliance on middlemen.
  • Skills grew as villagers learned to maintain the turbine, opening jobs in nearby valleys.

Big national grids are costly to build across mountains and isolated valleys. Small, local schemes — often called ‘intermediate technology’ or ‘appropriate technology’ — match the resources and needs of the community. They are cheaper, easier to repair locally and fit the geography. Schemes like Chambamontera show how renewable energy can leapfrog the fossil-fuel stage of development entirely, much as mobile phones leapfrogged landlines in many African countries.

Conclusion: A Sustainable Future

Across the last six lessons you have followed the UK from declining factories to a global service economy, looked at where food, water and energy come from, and seen the threat of insecurity at world scale. Chambamontera shows that the response can be local: a small turbine in a Peruvian valley brings electricity, jobs and dignity. The bigger picture — whether through North Sea wind farms, Indian solar parks, German heat pumps or Peruvian micro-hydro — is the same. Sustainable resource management is the central project of 21st-century geography.
exam_tip_html: For 6-mark and 9-mark case-study questions on a local renewable scheme, name the place (Chambamontera, Peru), state the scheme type (micro-hydro), and give specific impacts — e.g. ‘60 households powered, family income roughly £700–1,400 a year, kerosene replaced, local repair training’. For comparison-style questions, contrast renewables (low carbon, intermittent) with non-renewables (reliable, high emissions) using comparative connectives.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Renewable sources include wind, solar, hydro, tidal, wave, geothermal and biomass — all replenishing naturally and producing far less carbon than non-renewables.
  • Non-renewables (coal, oil, natural gas, uranium) still dominate global energy because of high density, existing infrastructure and on-demand reliability.
  • Chambamontera in Peru shows how a small micro-hydro scheme can lift around 60 households out of poverty by replacing kerosene, lighting homes and powering coffee processing.

glossary_terms.definition: Energy from sources that replenish naturally on a human timescale, such as wind, solar, hydro, biomass, geothermal, tidal and wave.
Energy from sources that take millions of years to form and cannot be replaced once used, such as coal, oil, natural gas and uranium for nuclear power.
A small-scale hydroelectric scheme that uses river flow to generate electricity for a single community, typically under 100 kilowatts.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a local renewable scheme can reduce poverty.
